title: The Water That Is Never Lacking: the Travesía of Caucete, the Child at the Breast, and the Roads of Argentina
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Angaco, and the War That Takes the Men

stops.name: Angaco, born in the years of the independence war
stops.date_confidence: undocumented. No birth record survives and no source names her birthplace; es.wikipedia says only that she was born during the wars of independence, which run 1810-1818. The date shown is the midpoint of that window, not a finding.
stops.campa: The province of San Juan lies against the eastern foot of the Andes, its life strung along irrigation ditches cut from snowmelt, and beyond the last ditch there is nothing but thorn and stone. Into this country a girl is born while the armies of the independence are still marching, and she is called Deolinda Correa. No parish book that survives carries her name. What survives instead is the shape of an ordinary life in the department of Angaco: the vine, the goats, the acequia, and the road that runs east into a desert nobody crosses without water.
suggested_refs: The parish registers of Angaco and Caucete, San Juan, searched since 2026 for any Correa baptism

stops.name: Angaco, the household of Clemente Bustos
stops.date_confidence: traditional. es.wikipedia states only that the family lived in the department of Angaco; no marriage date is given in any reachable source, and the year here is placed generically before the 1840 conscription.
stops.campa: She lives in Angaco with her husband Clemente Bustos and the family around them, some twenty kilometres northeast of the city of San Juan, where the green of the oasis gives out against the sand. Bustos is a countryman like every man on that ground, a rider who works other people's fields. There is a son at the breast. Nothing in the household is written down anywhere. That is the ordinary condition of the rural poor of Cuyo in these years: no deed to a property, and no page in any book that outlasts the people named on it.
suggested_refs: The oasis of Angaco and its department seat, Villa del Salvador, San Juan

stops.name: San Juan, the province divided between unitarios and federales
stops.date_confidence: attested as period context, not as an event in her life. The civil wars of Cuyo are documented; her family's relation to them is known only through the legend.
stops.campa: In the provincial capital the war between unitarios and federales is decided and undecided again, governors rise by acclamation and fall by the knife, and every faction that takes the city needs horsemen. The montonera is how the interior fights: mounted columns raised out of the countryside, taking their men where they find them. A levy does not ask. It rides into a department, names the men it wants, and rides out with them the same day. Angaco is a few hours from the plaza where these decisions are made, and it has men.
suggested_refs: The montonera warfare of Cuyo and La Rioja under the caudillos, 1820-1861

stops.name: Angaco, the levy takes Clemente Bustos
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year only. es.wikipedia gives 'hacia 1840' and names Bustos; en.wikipedia gives 'around the year 1840' and names nobody. No underlying muster roll or primary document is cited by either.
stops.campa: Around 1840 the recruiters come for Bustos and take him toward La Rioja with a montonera column. Word comes back that he has fallen sick on the march and been left behind by the troop. Deolinda hears it in a house with no man in it, an infant at her breast, and a desert lying between her and wherever he is lying. The tradition is exact about what she decides and silent about how long she takes to decide it. She goes after him on foot, with the child, along the road the column took.
stops.quote: alrededor del 1840 lo reclutaron a Bustos para ir a pelear en el enfrentamiento de unitarios y federales
stops.quote_source: La Capital (Rosario), 'La historia de la Difunta Correa, una santa popular a la que muchos le ofrecen agua', 17 February 2021
suggested_refs: The forced levies of the Cuyo montoneras, c. 1840

stops.name: Angaco, the alforjas and the two chifles
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated. es.wikipedia dates her death only to 'sometime in the 1840s'; the departure is placed here after the 1840 conscription.
stops.campa: She packs what the country gives: bread, charqui dried hard in the sun, and two chifles, the hollowed cattle horns that Cuyo carries water in. She ties the saddlebags, takes up the child, and steps out onto the track the column has left. She is following hoofprints across ground that keeps them well, because nothing grows there to cover them over. The chifles are the whole of the calculation. Two horns of water, one woman, one nursing infant, and a distance that nobody has measured because nobody walks it.
stops.quote: decidió preparar alforjas con dos 'chifles' de agua y provisiones, cargar a su hijo y emprender viaje
stops.quote_source: La Capital (Rosario), 'La historia de la Difunta Correa, una santa popular a la que muchos le ofrecen agua', 17 February 2021
suggested_refs: The chifle, the horn canteen of the Cuyo countryside

stops.name: Caucete, the last inhabited ground
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Caucete is the nearest town to the traditional site of her death; no source places her in it.
stops.campa: East of the city the cultivated land thins and ends at Caucete, and past Caucete the road gives out into the travesía, the dry crossing, where the water sits in wells that a traveller must already know about to find. Carts and mule trains cross it in timed stages with animals that can carry barrels. She crosses it walking. Behind her is the last house where she could have turned back and been fed. Ahead is a hundred kilometres of thorn and sand with nothing on it that throws shade except the algarrobo.
suggested_refs: The travesía east of Caucete, the dry crossing between the San Juan oasis and the llanos of La Rioja

stops.name: Chepes, the road east into La Rioja
stops.date_confidence: representative point, not a sourced location. The sources say only that the column marched toward La Rioja; no town on its route is named. Chepes stands here for the direction and the old camino real, not for a documented stage.
stops.campa: The column is marching toward La Rioja, and the old road east out of San Juan runs through the llanos toward Chepes and the interior beyond it. That is the direction she is walking. She does not know which camp holds him, or whether he is still in one, or whether he is alive. The war she is walking into is the war of the caudillos and the montoneras, fought across four provinces by men conscripted in one week and dead or deserted in the next, and nobody in it keeps a list of the sick left lying at the roadside.
suggested_refs: The camino real east out of San Juan toward the llanos of La Rioja

stops.name: Vallecito, the algarrobo
stops.date_confidence: traditional. es.wikipedia dates the death only to 'algún momento de la década de 1840'; 1840 is the year of the conscription, not of the death, and the two are frequently conflated. Month and day are unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: The water in the chifles gives out. She walks on into the heat with the child, and the heat of the travesía is a thing that kills healthy animals with barrels on them. At a place that has no name yet she stops in the only shade there is, under an algarrobo, and lies down. She dies there of thirst and exhaustion, still facing east, in the direction of the column. The child does not die. He goes on nursing at a body that has stopped, and he is still doing it when the next men come along the crossing.
stops.quote: Deolinda Correa, tras caminar por el desierto de Caucete cargando a su bebé en busca de su marido, fallece por deshidratación
stops.quote_source: Argentina.gob.ar (Presidencia de la Nación), 'Visitar el santuario Difunta Correa'
suggested_refs: The algarrobo of the travesía, the only shade tree of the Caucete desert

stops.name: Vallecito, the arrieros find the child alive
stops.date_confidence: sources conflict and the conflict is not resolved here. es.wikipedia, the fuller account, says arrieros passing 'al día siguiente' found her with milk still flowing; en.wikipedia says gauchos found her 'days later'. The next-day reading is followed for the date.
stops.campa: Arrieros come along the crossing driving their mules and see a woman lying under the algarrobo. She is dead. The infant at her breast is alive and feeding, and the milk, they say afterwards, is still coming. They take the child up with them and carry the account to the next settlement. What gets repeated there is not the death, which is common enough on that ground. It is the milk, and the boy who lived on it in a place that had already killed a grown woman.
stops.quote: Fue hallada sin vida, pero con su hijo aún amamantando
stops.quote_source: Argentina.gob.ar (Presidencia de la Nación), 'Visitar el santuario Difunta Correa'
suggested_refs: Chertudi and Newbery, La Difunta Correa (1978), the standard folkloric study behind the Spanish account

segments.name: The Grave, and What Became of the Child

stops.name: Vallecito, buried where she fell
stops.date_confidence: traditional. es.wikipedia says the arrieros buried her at the spot known today as Vallecito and took the child with them; the burial arrangements themselves are unrecorded.
stops.campa: The muleteers bury her at the place where they found her, in the ground she died on, and go on with the child. The place takes its name from the burial: Vallecito, the little valley. It is sixty-three kilometres east of the city of San Juan, on no map that matters to any authority and on every route that crosses the travesía. For a long time that is the whole of it, a mound in the scrub, known to the men who pass it because they pass it, and passed by nobody else at all.
suggested_refs: The grave site at Vallecito, Departamento Caucete, San Juan
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Santuario de la Difunta Correa, Ruta Nacional 141, Vallecito, Caucete)

stops.name: Vallecito, the first water left at the grave
stops.date_confidence: undated practice. en.wikipedia says miracles have been claimed at the site 'every year since its origins in 1840'; the water offering itself is not dated by any reachable source. The year here is a placeholder within that first decade.
stops.campa: Men crossing the travesía begin to stop at the grave. What they leave is water, because water is what she died without and because water is the thing they themselves are counting on for the next three days. The logic of the offering is exact and needs no theology behind it. She was thirsty, so she is given drink; and she is asked in return for the single thing she is qualified to grant, which is that whoever is walking this ground should not be left on it as she was.
stops.quote: A common votive offering is bottles of water 'to calm her eternal thirst'.
suggested_refs: The water offering at Vallecito, the founding votive practice of the cult

stops.name: San Juan, Plaza 25 de Mayo: the notice in El Zonda
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year. The advertisement is the only primary document either encyclopedia cites bearing on the family; the month and day are not given in any reachable summary and are defaulted.
stops.campa: Tradition names the rescued child Baudilio Bustos Correa. In 1865 a notice runs in the San Juan paper El Zonda, the sheet Domingo Faustino Sarmiento founded in this province and had revived three years before: a Baudilio Bustos Correa, living by the Plaza 25 de Mayo, is selling property before leaving for Córdoba. It is one advertisement in one provincial newspaper, and it is the only piece of paper anyone has ever produced that touches the family of the legend. Whether he is her son, the notice does not say.
suggested_refs: El Zonda, San Juan, 1865 issues of Sarmiento's revived paper; the original 1839 run lasted six numbers

stops.name: Vallecito, the adobe chapel of the arriero Zeballos
stops.date_confidence: undated. es.wikipedia names the arriero Zeballos as builder of the first chapel but gives no year; the date here is a placeholder in the late nineteenth century and should not be quoted as a finding.
stops.campa: An arriero named Zeballos builds the first chapel over the grave, adobe, the size of a room, roofed against the sun that killed her. He builds it in payment for something granted to him, and the tradition does not record what. A cross is a thing men pass and salute. A chapel is a thing men come to on purpose, with a candle and a request, having settled on the detour before they set out. After Zeballos, some of the people on that road have come out from San Juan for no other reason.
suggested_refs: The first adobe chapel at Vallecito, attributed to the arriero Zeballos

stops.name: Vallecito, the hilltop cross becomes a settlement
stops.date_confidence: attested to the decade. en.wikipedia dates the growth from the 1940s; the year is the decade's opening and no single founding event is recorded.
stops.campa: From the 1940s the place grows the way a town grows, without a plan and against the ground. Devotees who have been granted something come back and build: a chapel for a cure, a chapel for a road survived. Around the chapels come the stalls selling candles and images and cold drink, then the houses of the people who keep the stalls, then a school and a police post. The desert that killed her for want of one settlement now holds a settlement built entirely out of her death.
stops.quote: Since the 1940s, her shrine at Vallecito grew from a hilltop cross into a small town with a network of votive chapels (17 as of 2005), full of offerings.
suggested_refs: The village of Vallecito, Departamento Caucete, grown from the shrine

stops.name: Vallecito, the recumbent figure
stops.date_confidence: attested as present, undated as to installation. The sources disagree on which chapel holds it: es.wikipedia places the figure in the chapel said to contain her remains, en.wikipedia in the hilltop chapel. Not resolved.
stops.campa: In the chapel that is said to hold her remains lies a life-size figure of Deolinda, on her back, face turned up to the roof and to the sky beyond it, the child at her breast. She is not shown standing or crowned. She is shown at the moment the crossing fails, dead on the ground with the child feeding at her. The chapel around her is one of seventeen on the site and holds no relic that any authority has examined. Pilgrims put a hand on the plaster and talk to it, then set their bottles down and go back out into the light.
suggested_refs: The recumbent life-size image of the Difunta Correa at Vallecito

stops.name: Vallecito, seventeen chapels
stops.date_confidence: attested. The count of seventeen is given for 2005 by en.wikipedia; no later count was found in any reachable source.
stops.campa: By 2005 there are seventeen votive chapels standing on the site, each raised by whoever owed the debt, none of them ordered by any authority and none consecrated by one. Inside, the walls disappear behind what has been brought and left in thanks, hung so thickly that the surfaces of the buildings are no longer visible at all. Each object was carried out here by one person, in payment for one thing asked for on a road and afterwards received. There are seventeen buildings of it and no register anywhere of who left what.
suggested_refs: The seventeen votive chapels of the Vallecito sanctuary complex, counted in 2005

stops.name: Vallecito, a million in a year
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2005. es.wikipedia ties the million-a-year average explicitly to 2005. The Holy Week peak is given as 200,000 by en.wikipedia and up to 300,000 elsewhere; both figures are reported without a measuring year.
stops.campa: The counting begins once the crowds become a matter for the province. By 2005 the estimate is a million people a year arriving at Vallecito, with the great concentrations at Holy Week, when the figure given runs from two hundred thousand to three hundred thousand across a few days, and again at the Day of Souls on the second of November. They come by bus and by truck and on horseback, over roads laid down for the trade that first carried her name out of the desert.
stops.quote: se alza el Santuario de la Difunta Correa; un destino de fe y tradición que convoca a más de un millón de peregrinos cada año
stops.quote_source: Argentina.gob.ar (Presidencia de la Nación), 'Visitar el santuario Difunta Correa'
suggested_refs: Provincial visitor counts for the Vallecito sanctuary, 2005

stops.name: Mecca, the measure of a pilgrimage
stops.date_confidence: comparative anchor, not an event. The Kaaba is carried here as the reference point for mass votive pilgrimage; no claim is made that anyone connected to the legend travelled to it.
stops.campa: Around the Kaaba the hajj assembles the largest yearly convergence of people on a single point of ground anywhere on earth, brought there by a commandment of scripture, an ordained clergy, and thirteen centuries of law. Vallecito is a clearing in the travesía sixty-three kilometres from a provincial capital. It has no scripture and no clergy, and no church has ever recognised it. It gathers a million people in a year, assembled out of single decisions to stop at a grave.
suggested_refs: The hajj at the Grand Mosque of Mecca, reference point for mass votive pilgrimage

stops.name: Vallecito, the Cabalgata de la Fe
stops.date_confidence: attested as an annual event held between April and May; es.wikipedia names it without giving a founding year. The date shown is a representative April.
stops.campa: Between April and May the riders come, the Cabalgata de la Fe, columns of men and women on horseback converging on Vallecito across the same ground the montoneras crossed. They arrive in troops, dusty, with saddlebags and led horses, and they water their animals at the sanctuary. The province's oldest way of moving is the one that brings them. What was once a levy riding out of a department to take its men away is now a column riding in, of its own accord, to a woman that levy killed.
suggested_refs: The Cabalgata de la Fe, the annual mounted pilgrimage to Vallecito

segments.name: The Water on the Roads of Cuyo

stops.name: Pocito, a street carrying her name
stops.date_confidence: the street exists and is mapped; its naming date is unknown and the year shown is a placeholder for the modern period.
stops.campa: South of the city of San Juan, in the department of Pocito, a residential street carries her name on its corner sign, among streets named for generals and for dates. The name is not there as a devotion. It is there as an address, the thing written on an envelope and printed on a utility bill and given to a driver who has never heard the story. In her own province she has passed out of the register of the miraculous and into the register of the municipality, which paints the sign and replaces it when it fades.
suggested_refs: Calle Difunta Correa, Quinto Cuartel, Pocito, San Juan
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Difunta Correa, Quinto Cuartel, Pocito, San Juan)

stops.name: El Portezuelo, La Rioja: a neighbourhood takes her name
stops.date_confidence: mapped feature of unknown naming date; the year is a placeholder for the modern period.
stops.campa: In La Rioja, in the department named for the caudillo Facundo Quiroga, a neighbourhood at El Portezuelo is called Difunta Correa. It sits along the corridor her husband's column is said to have marched, in the province the column was marching to. The department is named for a caudillo whose own montoneras raised their men off this ground by the method that took Bustos. The direction she died walking in has her name on it now, fixed to houses and street signs by the people who live behind them.
suggested_refs: Barrio Difunta Correa, El Portezuelo, Departamento General Juan Facundo Quiroga, La Rioja
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Difunta Correa, El Portezuelo, La Rioja)

stops.name: Los Colorados, the shrine on Ruta Nacional 74
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the late twentieth century.
stops.campa: On Ruta Nacional 74, in the dry interior of La Rioja, a wayside shrine stands at the edge of the asphalt with bottles set around it in rows. The traveller who stops here is doing what the arrieros did on the travesía, at speed, with an engine instead of mules, and for exactly the same reason. This stretch is long and hot and has nothing on it. The petition has not changed since the 1840s: that whoever is crossing this ground should get across it, and that the woman who did not should have her water.
suggested_refs: Wayside shrine to the Difunta Correa, Ruta Nacional 74, Los Colorados, Departamento Independencia, La Rioja
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Difunta Correa, Ruta Nacional 74, Los Colorados, La Rioja)

stops.name: Luján de Cuyo, the shrine on the Panamericana
stops.date_confidence: mapped sanctuary of unknown foundation date; placed generically in the modern trucking era.
stops.campa: On the Panamericana at Luján de Cuyo, where the approach to Mendoza gathers the freight of half the country before it turns west, a sanctuary to the Difunta stands beside the lanes. The trucks that stop here are going over the Andes into Chile. Their drivers are about to spend a day and a night on a road that shuts without warning in winter and kills the careless in summer. They leave bottles at the door, and they get back into the cab, and they go up.
suggested_refs: Santuario Difunta Correa, Panamericana, Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Santuario Difunta Correa, Panamericana, Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza)

stops.name: Potrerillos, the foot of the climb
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: The road up from Mendoza toward the cordillera passes Potrerillos and begins to climb in earnest, the river below on one side and the rock standing on the other. A shrine sits on the shoulder here, where the gradient starts. The drivers who stop are at the foot of the ascent, doing the arithmetic every carter on this road has done since there were carts on it: water, weight, distance, and the hour of the day at which the pass will be at its worst. They leave what they can spare of the first, on a shelf already crowded with it.
suggested_refs: Wayside shrine on the Carretera Libertador General San Martín at Potrerillos, Mendoza
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Difunta Correa, Potrerillos, Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza)

stops.name: Uspallata, the last shrine before the pass
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: At Uspallata the valley opens for the last time before the border. Beyond it the road goes up to the cumbre and over into Chile, and everything on this side of the pass is the last of its kind: the last fuel, the last hot food, the last shrine. The bottles are heaped here in quantity, left by drivers who have looked at the cloud sitting on the mountain and made an offering instead of an assessment. Her grave is far behind them, in a desert that most of them have never seen.
stops.quote: Es común al pasar por los santuarios ver grandes cantidades de botellas, estas generalmente tienen agua 'para que nunca le falte el agua a la Difunta'
stops.quote_source: La Capital (Rosario), 'La historia de la Difunta Correa, una santa popular a la que muchos le ofrecen agua', 17 February 2021
suggested_refs: Wayside shrine at Uspallata, Las Heras, Mendoza, last stop before the Chilean pass
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Difunta Correa, Uspallata, Las Heras, Mendoza)

stops.name: Vicuña, the sanctuary in the Elqui valley
stops.date_confidence: mapped sanctuary of unknown foundation date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: Over the cordillera and down the far side, in the Elqui valley of Chile's Coquimbo region, a sanctuary bears her name. The border did not stop her, because the border does not stop the trucks. The devotion travels in the cab with the driver and gets out where he does, and where enough drivers get out at the same place, somebody eventually builds a niche and sets a bottle inside it. Chile keeps a Difunta Correa who died in a country most of her Chilean devotees have never entered.
suggested_refs: Santuario de la Difunta Correa, Vicuña, Región de Coquimbo, Chile
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Santuario de la Difunta Correa, Vicuña, Coquimbo)

stops.name: Copiapó, the shrine in the Atacama
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: North of Coquimbo the road runs into the Atacama, the driest desert on the planet, where in places no rain has been recorded within living memory. On Ruta 5 outside Copiapó there is a shrine to her. Of every place her name has reached, this is the one that most resembles the account of her death, allowing for the fact that she died five hundred kilometres away and never crossed the mountains at all. The offering here is water, in the landscape on earth that has least of it.
suggested_refs: Wayside shrine on Ruta 5 Norte, Copiapó, Región de Atacama, Chile
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Difunta Correa, Ruta 5 Norte, Copiapó, Atacama)

stops.name: Cauquenes, the chapel in the Maule
stops.date_confidence: mapped shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: South of Santiago, in the Maule region, a small chapel to the Difunta stands at Cauquenes, in the San Sebastián district, well off the Andean freight corridor, in green country where nobody has ever died of thirst. This is the far south of her reach in Chile, and there is no freight route to explain it. The chapel stands among houses rather than at a roadside, and the woman of the travesía is asked in it for things that have nothing to do with roads at all.
suggested_refs: Difunta Correa chapel, San Sebastián, Cauquenes, Región del Maule, Chile

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the devotion reaches the capital
stops.date_confidence: undated diffusion. es.wikipedia describes the spread outward from Cuyo without dates; the year is a placeholder for the era of large internal migration.
stops.campa: The capital receives her the way it receives everything from the interior, carried in by the people who come to work in it. Migrants from San Juan, La Rioja, and Catamarca bring her south, and the drivers keep her along the routes between. In a city with a cathedral on its central square she acquires shrines that nobody authorised, on pavements that nobody consecrated. Nobody here decides to adopt her. She arrives in the luggage of people moving in, and the shrines go up where they settle.
stops.quote: los devotos le llevan botellas con agua como símbolo
stops.quote_source: Argentina.gob.ar (Presidencia de la Nación), 'Visitar el santuario Difunta Correa'
suggested_refs: Internal migration from Cuyo and the northwest to Buenos Aires, twentieth century

stops.name: Justo Daract, the sanctuary on the main line
stops.date_confidence: mapped sanctuary of unknown foundation date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: On the motorway across San Luis, the main line between Buenos Aires and Mendoza, a sanctuary stands at Justo Daract where the traffic of the whole country goes past. This is the busiest ground her name occupies. Cars going on holiday stop here as well as trucks, and the offering has become a thing families do with children watching, an explained gesture, the story told over again in the front seat before the doors are opened. Nobody has to believe much of it for the bottle to be left.
suggested_refs: Santuario Difunta Correa, Autopista de las Serranías Puntanas, Justo Daract, San Luis
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Santuario Difunta Correa, Justo Daract, San Luis)

stops.name: Rufino, the shrine on the Ruta del Desierto
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: On Ruta Nacional 33 in Santa Fe, a road that still carries the name Ruta del Desierto out of an older frontier, a shrine to the Difunta stands among the truck stops of the wet pampa. There is no desert here. The land is black soil and standing water and some of the richest farmland on the continent. The shrine keeps the memory of a thirst this ground has never once imposed on anybody, on a road that carries the name of a desert that was never here either.
suggested_refs: Wayside shrine on Ruta Nacional 33, Rufino, Santa Fe
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Difunta Correa, Ruta Nacional 33 Ruta del Desierto, Rufino, Santa Fe)

stops.name: Capilla del Monte, the memorial on Ruta 38
stops.date_confidence: mapped memorial and bus stops of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: On Ruta Nacional 38 through the Punilla valley in Córdoba, a memorial to her stands beside a pair of bus stops that carry her name. The stops are named for her because the shrine was there first, and the timetables were printed afterwards. The provincial bus network now contains a dead woman from San Juan. Passengers waiting in the shade of the sign are waiting at her, whether or not they know it, and a few of them leave a bottle while they wait for the bus to Córdoba.
suggested_refs: Difunta Correa memorial and bus stops, Ruta Nacional 38, Capilla del Monte, Córdoba
sources: nominatim.openstreetmap.org (Difunta Correa memorial and bus stops, Capilla del Monte, Córdoba)

stops.name: Chacarita, the sanctuary on Avenida Corrientes
stops.date_confidence: mapped sanctuary of unknown foundation date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: On Avenida Corrientes at Chacarita, within reach of the great cemetery, a sanctuary to the Difunta Correa stands in the densest grid in the country. There is no crossing to survive on Corrientes and no water to run out of. What is asked here is work, health, a rent paid, a person come home safe. The shrine keeps the form of the desert petition and has emptied it of the desert, and the bottles are still set down on the pavement, by people on their way to a bus.
suggested_refs: Santuario de la Difunta Correa, Avenida Corrientes, Chacarita, Ciudad de Buenos Aires

stops.name: Batán, the sanctuary near the Atlantic
stops.date_confidence: mapped sanctuary of unknown foundation date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: At Batán, outside Mar del Plata, a sanctuary to the Difunta stands on Avenida Presidente Perón within a short drive of the Atlantic. A woman who died of thirst is petitioned here by people who live beside more water than they can see the end of. Nobody at the shrine finds that strange. What they ask her for is the road survived and the house reached at the end of it, and what they leave for it is what has always been left here: a bottle, set down full.

segments.name: To the Ends of the Roads

stops.name: Eldorado, the sanctuary among the yerba
stops.date_confidence: mapped sanctuary of unknown foundation date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: On Ruta Nacional 12 in Misiones, among the yerba plantations and the red earth of the subtropical north, a sanctuary to the Difunta Correa stands in a province that rains all year round. This is the far edge of her reach in that direction, fourteen hundred kilometres from the algarrobo, in a climate that contradicts every particular of her story. The bottles are left in a place where no one could possibly need them, by drivers who learned the practice somewhere drier and never stopped doing it.

stops.name: Villa Vil, the shrine on the Cuesta de Randolfo
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: On the Cuesta de Randolfo in western Catamarca, where the road climbs in switchbacks with a drop on the outside and no barrier along it, a shrine to the Difunta marks the worst of the ascent. Drivers stop before they start up. The surface is unpaved in long stretches and goes soft after rain, and there is no room on it for two vehicles to pass, and vehicles have been lost off the edge of it. The shrine stands at the last place on the ascent where a driver can pull over and think about that.

stops.name: Antofagasta de la Sierra, the shrine on the puna
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: High on the Catamarca puna, near the Chilean border, a wayside shrine to her stands on the provincial road among salt flats and volcanic cones, in air too thin to work in and cold enough at night to kill a man sleeping out. Almost nobody lives here. The traffic is mining trucks and the occasional pickup, and the gaps between fuel are measured in hundreds of kilometres. On this ground water is freight, hauled up from below with everything else, and a bottle left at the shrine is a bottle the driver has decided not to keep.

stops.name: Senillosa, the sanctuary on Ruta 22
stops.date_confidence: mapped sanctuary of unknown foundation date. The migration route is attested in general terms by es.wikipedia, which ties the southward spread to petroleum work; the shrine itself is undated.
stops.campa: On Ruta Nacional 22 in northern Patagonia, where the road runs the length of the Alto Valle between the orchards and the oil country, a sanctuary to the Difunta Correa serves the heaviest freight route in the south. The families who brought her down here came for the wells. Petroleum work pulled labour out of Cuyo and the northwest into Neuquén, Chubut, and Santa Cruz across the twentieth century, and the men who came brought their saint along with their tools.

stops.name: El Calafate, the shrine beside Lago Argentino
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period.
stops.campa: On the provincial road beside Lago Argentino, within sight of ice, a shrine to the Difunta Correa stands in the far south of the continent. The wind here takes roofs off buildings. The distances between settlements are the longest in the country, and the road is the only thing standing between a driver and the weather. Nothing here matches the desert except the fact underneath it: a person alone out on this ground can die of it, and knows so. The bottles are left in the lee of the shrine, where the wind cannot take them.

stops.name: Río Grande, the southernmost water
stops.date_confidence: mapped wayside shrine of unknown date; placed generically in the modern period. The distance figures are calculated, not quoted: roughly 2,455 km great-circle from Vallecito and something over 3,000 km by road.
stops.campa: On Ruta Nacional 3 at Río Grande, on the island of Tierra del Fuego, stands the last shrine of the line. Nearly two and a half thousand kilometres in a straight line from the algarrobo, and something over three thousand by the roads these drivers actually take, the practice reaches the end of the country and stops, because the land does. A woman who died walking perhaps a hundred kilometres from her own door has been carried the length of the continent by people going somewhere on wheels.

stops.name: Vallecito, the petition carried to Rome
stops.date_confidence: contradictory and unresolved. es.wikipedia dates the handover to January 2020 'during World Youth Day in Panama', but that gathering was held 22-27 January 2019 and no Panama edition took place in 2020; the news item it cites is dated 2 January 2020 and is now unreachable. Read as c. 2019-2020.
stops.campa: The Fundación Vallecito, which keeps the sanctuary, draws up a request that Rome open a cause of beatification for Deolinda Correa and puts it into the hands of Pope Francis himself, an Argentine who has known these roadside devotions his whole working life. The request asks the church to say formally what the country has been saying informally for a century and a half. Rome does not answer it. No cause is opened, and the chapels go on being built while none is.
suggested_refs: The Fundación Vallecito petition for the beatification of Deolinda Correa, c. 2019-2020

stops.name: San Juan, the Archdiocese opens the question
stops.date_confidence: attested, cross-verified. Reported by Diario de Cuyo (Estela Maris Ruiz) on 19 May 2026 and by Los Andes on 21 May 2026, the latter giving the three-year duration. The academic partner is the Instituto de Historia Regional y Argentina 'Héctor Domingo Arias', Facultad de Filosofía, UNSJ.
stops.campa: In May of 2026 the Archdiocese of San Juan and the regional history institute of the National University of San Juan announce a joint investigation, planned to run three years, into a single question: whether Deolinda Correa existed. Priests and academic historians go into the parish books, the notarial protocols, and the newspapers of the 1840s, looking for a woman whose devotees have never once required her to be documented before leaving water for her.
stops.quote: En el peor de los casos, que no tuviéramos finalmente documentos en mano que prueben fehacientemente su existencia, tampoco estaríamos habilitados para decir que Deolinda Correa no existió, simplemente estaremos habilitados para decir 'no encontramos'
stops.quote_source: Presbítero José Juan García, coordinator of the joint UNSJ and Archdiocese investigation, in Diario de Cuyo, 19 May 2026
suggested_refs: The 2026 UNSJ and Arzobispado de San Juan historical verification project, Instituto 'Héctor Domingo Arias'
sources: Diario de Cuyo, Estela Maris Ruiz, 19 May 2026

stops.name: Vallecito, the water goes on being left
stops.date_confidence: present-day condition, attested by both encyclopedias and by the May 2026 press coverage: she remains uncanonized and the devotion is undiminished.
stops.campa: Whatever the archives hold, the traffic does not pause for the finding. Buses arrive at Vallecito, riders arrive, trucks pull off Ruta 141 and their drivers walk up to the chapels with a bottle in each hand. The formal position is unchanged and everybody knows it: she is not a saint, because no church has ever said she is. The country has arranged the matter differently. She was thirsty, the child lived, and nobody crossing that ground is going to pass her without leaving something to drink.
stops.quote: Es una tradición oral que se ha transmitido muy fuerte y conlleva muchos valores morales también. Estaremos hablando de la fidelidad en el matrimonio al marido de parte de Deolinda, del cuidado del hijo, de la comunión en familia
stops.quote_source: Presbítero José Juan García, in Diario de Cuyo, 19 May 2026
suggested_refs: The Vallecito sanctuary on Ruta Nacional 141, Departamento Caucete, San Juan
